frameworks.name: Value Equation
frameworks.definition: A four-factor model for evaluating offer attractiveness: Dream Outcome x Perceived Likelihood of Achievement / Time Delay x Effort and Sacrifice. Increasing the numerator or decreasing the denominator increases perceived value.

frameworks.name: Quarterly Cleanup
frameworks.definition: A recurring email monetization cadence (once per quarter) that routes non-buyers through a freshly named challenge or lead magnet, varying the wrapper while keeping the core offer constant, to extract latent revenue from an existing list without fatiguing it.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi reports that one email campaign sent to 464,000 subscribers in a portfolio company's 3.3-million-person list generated $2.4 million in total revenue in five days: $1.6 million from an 8% conversion rate on a $2,000 offer, plus $800,000 from 20% of buyers ascending to an $8,000 upsell.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Consumer-facing business relying predominantly on paid ads
Email list built over several years with both buyers and non-buyers
Sub-segment of 15% of list targeted for test
Seven-day challenge used as the conversion mechanism
claims.mechanism: The seven-day challenge re-engaged dormant leads with zero additional CAC; all resulting gross profit fell directly to the bottom line because email acquisition cost is $0 once the lead exists.

anchors.region: Core $2,000 offer (800 buyers at 8% of 10,000 registrants)

bounded_by: List was warm (prospects knew the brand) rather than true cold
Results from a 15% sub-segment test, not the full list

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that email list revenue drops straight to the bottom line because the cost to acquire a customer via email is effectively zero once the lead is already captured, regardless of the original paid-media CAC.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Lead already captured via paid or other acquisition channel
Business has an existing email list with non-buyers
claims.mechanism: CAC on email re-engagement is $0 because the lead acquisition cost was already sunk; therefore the full gross profit on any email-driven sale adds to net profit rather than being consumed by acquisition cost.

anchors.region: Paid ads (primary channel for this business)

bounded_by: Applies only to leads already in the owned email list
Does not apply to cold email to purchased lists where CAN-SPAM compliance costs and list acquisition are real costs

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that consistent email sales make a business more attractive to investors because, unlike paid-ad revenue, an email list size does not change overnight, creating a stable and predictable revenue floor that smooths volatility.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business valued on a multiple of bottom-line profit (approximately 95% of businesses per Hormozi's claim)
Business has a large, established email list
claims.mechanism: Email-driven sales contribute directly to EBITDA without new CAC; stable EBITDA base lifts enterprise value on standard profit multiples. Additionally, list size is structurally stable (unlike ad performance), reducing revenue variance that investors discount.
bounded_by: Businesses valued on revenue multiples (SaaS) benefit differently
Assumes list hygiene and deliverability are maintained

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that 95% of businesses are valued on a multiple of bottom-line profit, which means email-driven zero-CAC sales are a direct multiplier of enterprise value, not just of revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Standard private-market business valuation

numbers.axis: Share of businesses valued on bottom-line multiples

anchors.region: Businesses valued on other multiples (e.g., SaaS revenue multiples)

bounded_by: SaaS and high-growth venture-backed companies typically valued on revenue, not profit

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's seven-day challenge generated $6 of revenue per email address from the 464,000-person sub-segment, which he uses as the unit metric to project what running the same campaign quarterly across the full 3.3-million-person list would yield.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Consumer business with large paid-ads-built email list
Warm (non-buyer but brand-aware) audience sub-segment
Seven-day challenge as conversion mechanism
Funnel: 18% open rate -> ~12% click-to-register of openers -> 8% purchase of registrants

numbers.axis: Revenue per email address in campaign sub-segment

anchors.region: Second run to different sub-segment (next month)

bounded_by: Metric applies to the sub-segment tested; full-list yield may differ due to list composition and fatigue

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines a good lead magnet as a complete solution to a narrow problem that, once solved, creates the next problem which the primary offer then solves; challenges satisfy this definition better than most formats because they deliver a time-bound, credible mini-outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business with an offer whose outcome takes significant time or effort
Audience that needs trust-building before purchase
claims.mechanism: A solved mini-problem installs a belief (I can achieve this), a behavior (I took action and was rewarded), and an interaction (the brand delivered); together these shift the prospect from skeptic to buyer of the primary offer.
bounded_by: Lead magnets that solve a problem unrelated to the primary offer do not create the next-problem bridge

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that challenges approximate brand for businesses that lack an established brand, compressing what would normally be a six-month relationship-building period into seven days by rapidly accumulating micro-interactions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Direct-response businesses without an established brand
Cold or dormant audience that has not consumed significant prior content from the creator
claims.mechanism: Brand functions as accumulated trust from repeated interactions; a challenge front-loads those interactions into a short window, giving the prospect a simulation of the relationship that a large back-catalog of content provides organically.
bounded_by: Audiences already deeply familiar with the brand's content require less trust-building via challenge; the challenge's incremental value is lower for them

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the number of offers made to a prospect is directly correlated with the revenue generated from that prospect, subject to the constraint that each offer reduces accumulated goodwill and therefore requires proportional value deposits to sustain the relationship.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to owned-list email or organic content distribution
Prospect has had prior brand exposure
claims.mechanism: Each sale ask debits goodwill; each piece of genuine value deposits goodwill. Net goodwill above zero enables the next ask. A list with many value deposits and few asks can sustain a burst of offers; a list with many asks and few deposits churns.
bounded_by: Does not apply to cold outreach where no goodwill exists yet

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the same offer sold through different mediums (email, phone, webinar, live in-person, book, course) commands different price points and triggers independent goodwill assessment by the prospect, allowing a business to re-offer without triggering offer fatigue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Same core information or service delivered
Different delivery medium used for each subsequent offer
claims.mechanism: Prospects judge their relationship with a brand medium-by-medium, not offer-by-offer in the abstract; switching medium resets perceived novelty even if the underlying content or offer is substantially the same.

numbers.axis: Price point by delivery medium for identical educational content

bounded_by: Commodity products with no relationship component (e.g., physical goods) do not exhibit medium-dependent goodwill segmentation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends running quarterly email conversion campaigns on sub-segments (10% of list or smaller) before scaling to the full list, because early test runs surface messaging and funnel errors that would otherwise waste the entire list's attention in one shot.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has a large email list (tens of thousands or more)
Campaign is new or untested
Goal is to convert non-buyers through a challenge or lead magnet
claims.mechanism: Small test run preserves the majority of list attention for the optimized version; split-testing subject lines, CTAs, and landing pages on a 10% segment can double or triple throughput before the full-list send.

numbers.axis: List percentage for test vs. full deployment

bounded_by: Very small lists (under 10,000 subscribers) may not have enough statistical power to benefit from sub-segment testing

claims.text: Alex Hormozi found that renaming or rewrapping a challenge each quarter (changing headline, landing page, and challenge name while keeping core deliverables the same) prevents list fatigue among non-buyers who did not convert in prior quarters.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Non-buyer re-engagement campaigns run multiple times per year
Audience has seen at least one prior version of the offer
claims.mechanism: Non-buyers self-select out of an offer partly due to the framing and wrapper, not only the underlying deliverable; changing the name and seasonal angle changes the perceived offer, re-qualifying prospects who rejected the prior framing.
bounded_by: Does not apply to buyers who already converted; repeated rewrapping does not generate additional purchases from converted customers without a distinct upsell

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the email campaign conversion funnel for a seven-day challenge to a warm non-buyer list produced: 18% open rate, approximately 12% click-to-register of openers, and 8% purchase rate of registrants, resulting in 10,000 registrants and 800 buyers from 464,000 emails sent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Consumer business with brand-aware (warm) non-buyer list
Seven-day challenge as the conversion mechanism
$2,000 price point on the primary offer
bounded_by: These metrics reflect a first-run campaign; repeated runs with split-test optimization are expected to improve each stage
Audience was warm (brand-aware non-buyers), not true cold traffic

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that trusting a team member's recommendation even when the leader disagrees is rational when the team member is closer to the relevant data, because at significant business scale (approaching $10 million per month) the CEO or investor cannot be the closest person to every data stream.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business operating at substantial scale (example given: approaching $10M/month)
Team member with relevant domain expertise and proximity to the data
claims.mechanism: In large organizations, data is distributed across functions; leaders receive summaries not raw signals. The person closest to the data has an informational advantage on tactical decisions; blocking their ideas without counter-evidence destroys that information advantage and, as a secondary effect, suppresses future idea generation from the team.
bounded_by: Applies to tactical decisions with recoverable downside (brand-safe, non-capital-intensive); irreversible or brand-damaging decisions require higher leader involvement regardless of proximity

examples.text: A portfolio company in Alex Hormozi's Acquisition.com portfolio runs predominantly on paid ads and had accumulated a 3.3-million-person email list over several years without systematically monetizing it beyond initial-purchase follow-up sequences. When paid-ad performance declined and quarterly revenue targets were at risk, the marketing director proposed a seven-day challenge sent to a 464,000-person sub-segment. Hormozi and the CEO were skeptical but deferred to the marketing director. The campaign generated 10,000 registrants, 800 buyers at $2,000, and 160 upsells at $8,000, totaling $2.4 million in five days. The team then ran the identical play to a different sub-segment the following month and generated $2.2 million, confirming the repeatability of the mechanism.

Alex Hormozi describes his Gym Launch experience rewrapping the same fundamental fitness and nutrition challenge under a rotating series of names tied to seasons and life events: Six-Week Challenge, 42-Day Fix, 42-Day Transformation, Six-Week Booty Blast, Slim for Santa, Lean by Halloween, Slim for Summer, Accountability Buddy Challenge. The underlying deliverable in each case was eating less and moving more, but the seasonal wrapper and named pain point allowed the same offer to be re-promoted to the same local audience repeatedly without triggering the fatigue that a repeated identical campaign would cause.

Alex Hormozi uses a weight-loss business as an illustrative example for lead magnet design: instead of promising the full long-term transformation (which takes months), the business offers a seven-day cleanse where participants lose seven pounds (mostly water weight). Participants are excited by the fast result, have taken action, received behavioral reward, and interacted with the brand — all of which align them toward purchasing the long-term program. The mini-outcome creates belief and momentum, not just awareness.

Alex Hormozi describes the School Games as his version of a challenge: a 14-day free experience where participants are walked step-by-step through starting a business online, with leaderboards, prizes, and live calls from Hormozi himself. He reports that just under one in three participants earns their first dollar within the first month, which he uses as the conversion signal that leads participants to believe they can make more dollars — creating readiness for a paid offer.

practices.text: Maintain a regular email cadence (beyond initial purchase follow-up) to preserve domain reputation and deliverability; even value-only emails between promotional campaigns serve this technical function.
Before the first full-list campaign deployment, run two to three sub-segment tests (10% of list or smaller each) to optimize subject lines, CTAs, landing page headlines, and the challenge name.
Build one annual promotional calendar with four quarterly challenges or lead magnets; once the calendar is validated, keep it on autopilot rather than inventing new concepts each year.

When a team member is significantly closer to the data on a tactical decision and the downside is recoverable, extend trust and let them run the experiment rather than blocking based on leader intuition alone.

Position email as a 401k-style asset: daily ad spend or outbound is the paycheck (direct effort to direct return); the email list is the investment account that compounds over time if contributed to consistently.
